Development guide

Project Discovery

Decide which problem to solve, test possible solutions and use the evidence to choose what to build.

Use these six steps with Product, Design and Engineering to choose the next learning or delivery investment. Start with a user problem, an existing finding or an uncertain capability; you do not need a settled solution. An asset management journey applies each decision, technique and method, from the spreadsheet problem to a bounded application pilot.

Learning example · Problem background

Maya, a project manager, tracks equipment assignments in a spreadsheet. Alex and the other project members have to ask her to update it when something changes. Maya also organises the annual asset check by hand.

Follow the team as it investigates the problem and tests an application that lets members:

  • report a handover to another member;
  • report equipment that is lost or faulty;
  • complete a scheduled annual declaration.

A declaration records which assets a member holds and whether they work. “Custody” means who currently holds an asset. The starting problem comes from the supplied brief; the people, research and results are fictional. Product, Design and Engineering form the delivery team. Maya and the members use the application.

Start together: Product, Design and Engineering

Product, Design and Engineering investigate the problem and compare possible responses together. Any discipline can initiate Project Discovery. Begin with the evidence before fixing a solution, and keep all three perspectives involved as findings change the direction.

Basis: SVPG’s four-risk guidance [3] calls for collaborative problem solving; its guidance on research and delivery [10] describes Product, Design and Engineering working side by side.

Bring different expertise to the same problem

  • Product: investigate who benefits, which outcome matters, and whether the idea creates value within business constraints. Connect priorities and investment choices to the evidence.
  • Design: investigate how people carry out the task, where they struggle and whether they can use the proposed solution. Shape and test the complete experience, including failure and recovery.
  • Engineering: investigate what is technically possible with the available time, skills and technology. Explore alternatives and test uncertain capabilities, integrations, permissions and operating costs early.

These areas of expertise overlap: all three help frame the problem, generate options and interpret findings. Map the responsibilities to local roles and involve research, testing, operations, security and other specialists as needed.

Use shared source notes and test results to record what changed, where the team disagrees and what to investigate next.

Keep a short concept brief linked to the experiment and decision records. Develop the product requirements document (PRD) together as intended behaviour becomes clearer. The authorised decision owner makes the investment decision using the team’s evidence; collaboration does not replace local approval authority.

Torres’s opportunity-tree guidance [8] describes mapping research findings as a team activity for Product, Design and Engineering. Sheth’s “3-in-a-Box” proposal [5] emphasises continuous co-creation around intent, interaction and implementation.

AIHow AI can help

Keep AI assistance connected to evidence

Use AI to support the team’s research, prototypes and technical tests. Give each task a question, permitted inputs, an expected output and a reviewer. When an AI agent uses tools to carry out several steps, set its permissions before it starts. Label observations, AI interpretations and untested suggestions separately, and check original sources before relying on a generated claim.

Related reading: Product School’s guide to AI-supported research [15]. NIST’s Generative AI Profile [17], action MS-2.5-003 and Appendix A.1.6, support checking generated citations and retaining content provenance.

Product reviews the spreadsheet problem and the walkthrough of the asset register. It recommends investing in more accurate records and reliable follow-up. AI can draft alternative ways to achieve that outcome.

Design watches members report asset changes and Maya review the annual check. It looks at how people:

  • hand an asset to another member;
  • report an asset that is lost or faulty;
  • find and act on reports that need follow-up.

AI can suggest clearer wording for these choices. Design checks that the wording matches what users need to report.

Engineering uses a test environment to check:

If the team later adds AI to help draft or sort fault reports, specialists check its suggestions against reports kept separate from development. They check how sensitive details are handled and whether the scoring method is reliable. The core application and annual schedule follow predefined rules.

Learning example · Data access and decision authority

Risk and compliance specialists confirm:

  • which project and member records each role may access;
  • how long the records may be kept;
  • who may authorise inspections and repairs.

AI can link reviewed evidence to the relevant controls. Specialists check those links.

AgentsNo organisational accountabilityResearch, challenge, specification drafting, prototyping, testing and evaluation

Learning example · The agent’s permitted work

An agent can draft a reporting prototype and test the annual workflow in an isolated environment. People still decide whether to fund the pilot and confirm physical inspections. The agent needs separate authorisation to access the live register.

For this to work, the shared environment needs:

  • access to current, relevant product and technical context;
  • clear ownership, permissions and decision authority;
  • visible agent activity, sources, outputs and status;
  • a structured route for review, feedback and exceptions; and
  • explicit human approval for high-consequence decisions.

Review technical limits alongside user needs before investing in a solution.

Read about delegated work and review capacity.

Source: [1], “Structure the team right”, on named accountability and multidisciplinary teams.

Follow the learning cycle

Project Discovery asks whether a problem is worth solving and whether a proposed solution earns further investment. In the AI-Software Development Lifecycle (AI-SDLC), implementation turns that intent into verified software and returns new learning.

Start with the decision you need to make

Start with a user or business problem, an obligation, or a new capability whose value is uncertain. Bring existing observations, alternatives and constraints, and name the person responsible for collecting evidence. Return to Project Discovery when research, incidents or delivery findings challenge the intended outcome. Send well-understood defects directly to implementation.

Choose the entry point from the uncertainty. If the problem is unclear, start at step 1. If existing evidence supports the need, use step 2 to compare responses. If a concept already has credible support, use step 3 to test its unresolved assumptions. Link the existing evidence and check that its users, conditions and constraints still apply.

Steps 3–5 form a short cycle: choose a test, run it, then decide what the findings justify. Repeat within the agreed budget. Decisions to investigate, change direction or stop can also follow problem research or an early comparison; there is no need to complete every step first. Scale the work to the consequences of the decision.

Business research examines need, value, adoption and affordability. Technical investigation tests whether a candidate solution can work within delivery and operating limits. Carry both throughout Project Discovery; a critical technical question can justify a test before the problem framing is complete.

Develop the brief and PRD as you learn

Keep records detailed enough for the next decision. A delivery slice is a small, useful scope the team can build and assess. Agree that scope from the evidence, then carry its requirements and remaining questions into implementation.

One evolving product intent, with increasing evidence
ArtefactPurpose and maturity
Concept brief (Frame)Why this user, problem and possible direction deserve investigation. Includes alternatives, baseline, assumptions and the next test; it is not an implementation-ready specification.
Draft PRD (when behaviour becomes concrete)Describe proposed behaviour, interaction states, constraints and provisional acceptance criteria: observable results the product should demonstrate. An interview, sketch or technical test can start from a question and experiment record. Develop the PRD when the test or delivery scope needs that detail, and link findings to the version examined.
Evidence-backed PRD (delivery slice)Versioned scope with linked evidence, user interface (UI) designs or application programming interface (API) examples, testable criteria and owners for open questions. It remains revisable; commitment is not production approval.

AI-assisted development uses AI to help research, draft, build or check software. An AI product uses AI at runtime; only products with agents taking or choosing actions need the optional agent-journey checks. People retain accountability in every case.

Follow the six journey panels in order, then continue with the same records in Product implementation. The method and framework references explore other ways to test this asset-management idea; they are options rather than extra pilot stages.

1. Frame and understand the problem

Product, Design and Engineering agree whose outcome they hope to improve and why it matters now. Treat that outcome as provisional until research supports it.

Learn whose task is failing and where the difficulty occurs before choosing a solution. Observe the workflow, speak with affected people and examine support or operational records. Separate observations from hypotheses: proposed explanations or expected results that still need testing.

Use 6W to investigate and 4C to check the statement

Use the Defence Product Playbook’s six questions (6W) [1] to investigate the problem before drafting the statement. Product, Design and Engineering bring together observations, interviews and operational records. For each answer, retain the source, date and any gap or disagreement.

  • What goes wrong? Describe the task, the result the user needs and the difficulty observed. Record how serious the difficulty is, using measures such as time, errors or unfinished work where available.
  • Where does it happen? Identify the service, environment and point in the workflow. Note whether the difficulty also occurs through other channels or systems.
  • When does it happen? Identify triggers and conditions, such as peak demand or a handover. Record how often it occurs and the period observed.
  • Who is affected? Name the user group and relevant differences in tasks, experience or access needs. Identify who is unaffected and where the research has not reached.
  • Why might it happen? List plausible causes and the evidence for or against each. Label untested explanations as hypotheses; a repeated complaint does not establish its cause.
  • Why does it matter? Explain the effect on users and the organisation if nothing changes. Quantify the consequence where evidence allows, and identify foreseeable risks or deadlines.

Draft a short statement naming the affected group, task, difficulty and consequence. Keep the supporting evidence and possible causes alongside it. Then use the four checks (4C) to decide what is clear enough to compare and what still needs investigation.

The 4C problem-statement check, adapted from the Defence Product Playbook
CriterionWhat the statement shows
ClarityCan a reader identify the user group, task and difficulty? Describe severity and frequency with a defined sample or period. Replace broad labels such as “inefficient” with observable behaviour.
ConsequenceWhat happens if the problem remains? Link time, cost, service impact or potential harm to evidence. Mark estimates and missing measures explicitly; do not invent a number to complete the statement.
CauseWhat could explain the difficulty, and how could changing that condition improve the outcome? Write this proposed link as a theory of change. Keep competing explanations visible until the evidence distinguishes them.
ConfirmationWhich observations or tests support the proposed cause, and which contradict it? Check the original records and their limits. Where the cause remains uncertain, name the next observation or test and its owner.

Record the revised statement, evidence links and unanswered questions in the Project Discovery brief. The team can compare a well-evidenced need while its cause is still uncertain, but keeps that uncertainty explicit when choosing solutions and tests.

Recognise four weak substitutes for a problem

The playbook identifies four statements that can start an investigation but leave the underlying problem unclear. The fictional examples below show what to ask next; use findings from your own research to write the problem statement.

Learning example · Incomplete problem statements

  • An aspiration: “We want complete asset accountability.” This describes a goal without explaining the difficulty. Ask who is struggling to account for equipment and what gets in their way. Record the current result before setting an improvement target.
  • A proposed solution: “We need an asset management app.” This chooses a solution before explaining the need. Ask people to show where the current reporting process fails. Keep the problem statement open to different responses, including changes to the process or existing tools.
  • An end-of-life notice: “The spreadsheet automation will lose support.” Ask the system owner when support ends and what will stop being maintained. Explain how that could affect the service and what could keep it running safely. A confirmed future risk can justify planning a replacement before users experience a failure.
  • A vague complaint: “Our asset spreadsheet is always out of date.” Ask a member to show a recent update that went wrong. Record what happened and how often similar problems occur. Keep that observation separate from explanations that still need checking.

To compare discretionary improvements, assess severity, frequency and reach (SFR): how serious the problem is, how often it occurs and how many people it affects. Score each low, medium or high, with evidence and uncertainty. Use the scores to inform the decision.

Consider mandatory obligations and unacceptable risks before ranking discretionary work. A rare problem may still demand action because of serious harm, security exposure, an accessibility barrier or failure of an essential service. Record the reason, urgency and decision owner.

Plan research around the next decision

Agree which decision the research will inform, what could change it and how much time and money to spend. For each question, name a source, method and owner. Review existing findings first, and recruit people with different tasks, experience and access needs.

  • Problem evidence: observe the current task and alternatives; record friction, consequences and exceptions with the source and date.
  • Starting measure (baseline): record the current outcome, how it is measured and who would benefit from improvement. Record gaps that prevent a credible comparison.
  • System context: ask system owners to demonstrate the relevant interfaces, permissions and failure behaviour. Mark unconfirmed capabilities as assumptions.
  • Findings: separate observations from explanations, retain contradictions and identify the next question. Decide whether the evidence supports comparing opportunities or requires further investigation.

Problem research follows the Design Council’s Discover and Define [2].

AIHow AI can help

Check AI summaries against the research

Use AI to group interview notes, support cases or observations into recurring issues. Before using the summary to choose a problem or solution, ask a reviewer to check it against the original records:

  1. Check what people actually said or did. For each finding that could affect the decision, link to the source passage, observation note or recording timestamp. Record the date and user group. Read the surrounding context and note evidence that disagrees with the summary.
  2. Check who and what was counted. Remove duplicate records and distinguish the number of people from the number of comments or incidents. Several comments from one person do not represent several users. Before reporting a trend, compare similar periods and feedback channels, and note changes in who contributed.
  3. Look for missing issues. Choose a sample of original records yourself, beyond those the AI cited. Check whether the summary missed different experiences, access needs or rare but serious problems. Review recordings or observation notes when a transcript leaves relevant behaviour unclear.
  4. Separate observations from explanations. Label what the research shows and what still needs testing. Ask system owners to check technical explanations against documentation or executable tests before treating them as facts.

Learning example · An unsupported AI summary

AI summarises the brief as “Members lose assets because spreadsheets are unreliable.” The brief says members lack a direct reporting route. It does not say how many assets are lost or why. Compare the claim with the original notes and the register walkthrough before relying on it.

Count a forwarded fault email and its original as one report. If the summary leaves out a member’s difficulty using the form, restore that finding. Design records what the notes support and what remains unclear. Engineering checks any proposed technical cause. Use the remaining question to choose the next observation or test.

Keep a reviewed summary: record the supported findings, source links, disagreements and unanswered questions. Use it to choose the next research question or technical test, name its owner, and revisit it when new evidence could change the decision.

Establish the system context

Engineering asks system owners to demonstrate the current workflow, data access, interfaces and known limits. Record confirmed constraints and untested claims beside the user evidence. If a blocker could rule out useful work, run a focused technical test now. As candidate responses emerge in step 2, use the technical investigation checklist to investigate their specific assumptions.

Asset management journey 1 of 6 · understand the problem

Learning example · Problem research

Start with a task people recognise. Alex hands a monitor to Priya, another project member. Later, he finds that his laptop is faulty. On another occasion, he cannot locate a docking station. Maya needs to hear about each change so she can update the register and arrange follow-up. A request to “build an app” does not explain why those updates are difficult.

Use the six questions to investigate the asset problem
QuestionWhat the team investigates
What goes wrong?What the team investigatesMembers cannot update the register directly. Trace recent reports from the member to Maya’s records:
  • a handover;
  • a lost item;
  • a fault.
Where does it happen?What the team investigatesFollow how a physical handover becomes a message and then a spreadsheet update. Include remote members and people who share equipment.
When does it happen?What the team investigatesLook at changes throughout the year and during the annual check. Include:
  • members joining or leaving;
  • assets changing hands;
  • reports of loss or faults;
  • changes made while an annual declaration is open.
Who is affected?What the team investigatesSpeak with members who hold equipment and managers who check records or arrange repairs. Include people with different access needs.
Why might it happen?What the team investigatesMembers have no direct way to record changes. Check possible contributing causes:
  • the missing reporting route;
  • unclear responsibility for recording handovers;
  • asset identifiers that people cannot reliably match to equipment.
Why does it matter?What the team investigatesMaya may chase someone who no longer holds an item or overlook a needed repair. Record:
  • delays in updating records;
  • work left unresolved;
  • time spent chasing people.
Use those observations before estimating cost or loss.

Apply the four checks to the problem statement.

  • Clarity: name the members and managers affected and explain the reporting gap;
  • Consequence: show how outdated records delay follow-up;
  • Cause: propose how direct reporting and scheduled annual checks could help;
  • Confirmation: identify which observations and tests support that explanation.

In the fictional walkthrough, the team checks 20 records with eight members. Six assignments name someone other than the current holder. Three fault reports appear in messages but not in the register. Keep the notes and record any overlap between these findings. This small sample cannot show how common the problem is across all projects.

Choose what to investigate next. The walkthrough gives the team a reason to investigate unrecorded changes. Each discipline follows up:

  • Design observes how members report changes and how Maya responds;
  • Engineering checks asset identifiers and update permissions;
  • Product records who is affected, how serious and frequent the difficulty is, and what remains unknown.

An urgent safety fault or an accessibility barrier can take priority even if it affects few people.

Output: Provisional outcome, evidenced problem statement, source notes, system constraints and unresolved causes. Next: Use step 2 to choose an opportunity and compare responses, or continue research if the need remains unclear.

2. Choose a user need and compare solutions

Make two choices together: which user need deserves further work, then which possible solutions deserve a test. Use the reviewed research and provisional outcome from step 1. If a new technology prompted the work, first establish a user need it could address.

An opportunity is a user need, pain point or desire that could help achieve the desired outcome when addressed. A concept describes one possible solution. See Teresa Torres’s definitions [8]. An outcome describes the useful change sought; an opportunity is a researched need that could contribute to it; solutions are alternative responses worth testing.

Select a user need for the next learning cycle

  1. Build a shortlist from the research. Group findings by user need, retaining distinct experiences and possible causes. For each opportunity, name the affected users, task, difficulty or foreseeable risk, consequence and evidence links.
  2. Compare importance and uncertainty. Product, Design and Engineering examine severity, frequency, reach, access needs, urgency and the expected contribution to the outcome. Record the baseline, gaps and contradictory findings. Keep obligations and unacceptable risks visible alongside discretionary improvements.
  3. Check what could prevent useful work. Record known constraints, dependencies and capabilities. Distinguish constraints that affect every response from cost or feasibility assumptions about a particular solution. Investigate a potential blocker before committing substantial effort.
  4. Record the choice and its limits. Select an opportunity for this learning cycle and name the decision owner. Explain why it takes priority, why others are deferred or rejected, and when or on what evidence the choice will be revisited. An important but uncertain need may justify further research before comparing solutions.

Use scores to make assumptions visible, rather than to manufacture precision. Keep mandatory obligations and intolerable risks explicit when they override discretionary priorities. Revisit the shortlist when new capabilities, constraints or evidence change the available choices.

Compare different ways to address the need

Product, Design and Engineering propose alternatives that differ in how they address the difficulty. Include the current workflow as a reference. Consider process or content changes, reusing or buying a capability, conventional software and AI where relevant.

Compare each option against the same users, task and intended outcome. Use existing findings, sketches, demonstrations or a small task-based comparison to examine expected benefit, user effort, access needs, technical constraints and build, run and support costs. Mark each conclusion as supported by evidence or still an assumption.

Record what each option could improve, what it leaves unresolved and the uncertainty most likely to change the choice. Select a concept for testing only when the team can explain what it needs to learn. If the options remain indistinguishable, plan a comparison in step 3. If the need itself is unclear, return to step 1.

Retain the alternatives and reasons in the concept brief. A simpler option may already meet the need, and rejecting one solution does not remove the opportunity.

AIHow AI can help

Check the assumptions behind priorities

Compare planned investment with actual effort, measured outcomes, obligations and dependencies. Use competitor research to suggest questions for users; a supplier’s launch announcement alone does not show what customers need.

Compare delivering sooner with testing the largest uncertainty first. Use the same intended outcomes and resource limits for both plans. Engineering checks dependencies, quality targets, operating cost and how easily the approach could change. Record what evidence would change the order of work.

For an AI-generated ranking, record the benefit, effort and dependency assumptions. Check whether plausible changes would reverse the ranking. Agreement across generated answers does not replace evidence.

Define success for the selected scope

Product, Design and Engineering agree how they will tell whether users benefit and the product creates value. Choose the measures during Project Discovery, test whether they can be collected, and carry them into the handoff measurement plan. Passing acceptance tests provides evidence that the tested behaviour meets the specification under the recorded conditions. Product measures help the team assess whether users benefit in practice.

A North Star metric is a main product measure of the value users receive, chosen for its expected connection to longer-term business results. Amplitude’s North Star Playbook [19] pairs it with a small set of measures the team can influence. For an internal service, this guide recommends relating that value to the organisation’s mission or service outcome.

  • Product direction: use the existing product North Star where it fits. Explain the link from the proposed change to that measure and the wider outcome. Avoid inventing a different North Star for every feature.
  • Success for this scope: choose an outcome the team expects this change to improve, such as reconciled asset custody and condition, timely fault follow-up or less manager chasing. Raw logins, clicks or declarations opened do not establish that benefit.
  • Supporting measures: track behaviours or capabilities expected to influence the outcome, such as acknowledged handovers, member reports reaching the manager queue or declarations submitted by the due date. Treat that relationship as a hypothesis to check. Amplitude calls these input metrics; they differ from resource inputs such as funding in the metric ladder below.
  • Guardrails: set limits on errors, security, privacy, accessibility, reliability, cost and review effort. A favourable headline result does not compensate for a breached limit.

Check that the main measure reflects useful outcomes, can be measured consistently and cannot improve merely by hiding failures or serving easier cases. Report relevant user groups and case types separately; one metric cannot represent every outcome or risk. If no credible North Star is established yet, record a provisional product outcome and how the team will test its usefulness; still define success for the proposed scope.

Assess access restrictions separately from average quality scores. An accurate asset record still fails the test if it exposes another project’s member or asset details. Finding no failures in a small test does not prove that failures are impossible.

The Defence Product Playbook [1] connects a value measure to a longer-term outcome. Torres [8] distinguishes product outcomes from feature adoption.

Measurement thread: outcome → metric definition and baseline → target and guardrails → experiment result → handoff → review after use. Keep definitions and evidence linked across the journey.

AIHow AI can help

Use AI differently when widening and narrowing

  • When widening, use AI to research broadly, summarise evidence, generate different concepts, surface hidden assumptions and explore alternative journeys or technical approaches.
  • When narrowing, compare options against user value, strength of evidence, feasibility, cost, risk and strategic fit. Do not choose an option because it is the most polished or the easiest to generate.

Keep source links beside research summaries and check them before using a claim. Treat generated personas, synthetic interviews and an agent’s critique as prompts for research, not observations of real users.

Challenge the proposal before refining it

AI can turn a stakeholder request into a polished specification quickly. That speed creates a risk: refining an idea nobody has challenged. Before commitment, ask a reviewer, or an agent instructed to act as a critic, to work through these questions:

  1. What evidence shows that the problem is important and severe enough?

    Learning example · Evidence of reporting difficulties

    The brief says members have no direct way to report changes. Walk through the register with them to check how often old assignments or delayed fault reports cause difficulty.

  2. What happens if the organisation does nothing?

    Learning example · The cost of keeping the current workflow

    Use the current spreadsheet, messages and manually arranged annual check as the starting comparison. Include the time Maya spends chasing replies and the cases still awaiting action.

  3. Which users experience the problem, and which do not?

    Learning example · Different users and access needs

    Check whose experience differs:

    • members who use equipment in the office;
    • members who work remotely or share equipment;
    • managers who maintain the register;
    • members with different access needs.

    Some projects may already have a system that meets their needs.

  4. Why this solution rather than a materially different one?

    Learning example · Alternative reporting solutions

    Compare three ways to collect and follow up reports:

    • a form with controlled access;
    • an existing asset platform configured for the project;
    • a dedicated application.

    Test the important differences before choosing what to build.

  5. Which assumption could invalidate the proposal?

    Learning example · Assumptions behind self-service reporting

    Can members identify the right asset? Will Maya have time to act on their reports? Test both assumptions: easier reporting helps only if it produces records people can use.

  6. What is the cheapest credible experiment that could disprove it?

    Learning example · A small test of the proposed workflow

    Test a small declaration flow with “not with me” and “faulty” choices. Separately, interrupt and retry the yearly background job in a test environment. These checks can reveal problems before the team builds the full application.

  7. Which requirements conflict, and what fails at much greater scale?

    Learning example · Conflicting goals and growing workloads

    A target of “everyone confirms every asset is working” could discourage honest reports. Test what happens when:

    • a member reports an asset that is missing or faulty;
    • many annual tasks and reminders run at once;
    • the number of reports exceeds the manager’s follow-up capacity.

This challenge complements user research and domain expertise; it does not replace them. Regulated, safety-critical, legally consequential and highly specialised questions still need qualified human reviewers.

Learning example · AI-assisted comparison of alternatives

Give AI the brief and the reviewed walkthrough notes, along with project rules it is permitted to use. Ask it to suggest ways members could report changes:

  • a form;
  • an existing asset platform;
  • a dedicated application.

Generated personas can help rehearse research questions, but they provide no observations of actual users.

Compare each suggestion on the same basis:

  • the outcome it could improve;
  • accessibility and permissions;
  • Maya’s workload;
  • build and operating costs;
  • technical limits.

Product records disputed assumptions. Design checks the complete user journey. Engineering reviews the test findings before the team recommends an investment.

Write a short concept brief

Before committing to delivery, write a concept brief explaining the problem, proposed solution and reasons to test it. Aim for one page with evidence links. Anyone in Product, Design or Engineering can draft it; the three refine it together.

The following is a suggested working format. Record:

  • User, problem and evidence: the target user, their task, the consequence of doing nothing, and linked observations, requests or analysis. Distinguish a request from evidence of its underlying need.
  • Outcome and value: the outcome the user needs, the value to the organisation and why the opportunity matters now.
  • Proposed direction and alternatives: the initial solution hypothesis, the expected interaction and the alternatives worth comparing.
  • Feasibility and boundaries: enabling capabilities, known constraints, exclusions, risks, dependencies and unresolved assumptions.
  • Reasons to change or stop: evidence or limits, agreed in advance, that would trigger a redesign, a pivot or a stop.

Name the brief’s owner, next experiment and decision owner. Share it with relevant stakeholders before seeking the next investment, then update it as evidence changes. Develop a draft PRD from this brief as the intended behaviour becomes clearer. Label assumptions and provisional criteria explicitly.

Asset management journey 2 of 6 · compare responses before committing

Learning example · Solution comparison

Separate the outcome from the solution. Maya needs an accurate register and a reliable way to follow up problems. Members need to report changes when they happen. An application is one way the team might meet those needs.

Compare ways to address the same reporting need
ResponseWhat to learn before choosing it
Keep the current workflowWhat to learn before choosing itUse the spreadsheet and messages as the comparison. Record how long changes wait and how much annual chasing Maya does.
Add a controlled form and remindersWhat to learn before choosing itCheck whether existing tools can:
  • collect member reports;
  • record acknowledged handovers;
  • maintain Maya’s follow-up queue.
Check that each option preserves history and limits access appropriately.
Configure an existing asset platformWhat to learn before choosing itCan the platform support this project’s roles and annual workflow? Check:
  • handling of reports that need follow-up;
  • data migration;
  • accessibility;
  • licensing and support costs.
Build a member-facing applicationWhat to learn before choosing itWould a single application make the complete task easier? Test how it connects:
  • the member’s assigned assets;
  • reports of changes;
  • annual declarations.
Compare any benefit with the cost of building and running it.

Four members and Maya compare three options in the fictional study:

  • The form records faults, but the trial leaves handover acknowledgement and annual follow-up unclear;
  • The platform demonstration leaves project-level access unconfirmed;
  • The paper application flow gives the team a candidate to test next.

Keep the form and platform as alternatives while investigating the application.

Write a short concept brief. Explain the reporting problem and expected value. Include:

  • the users and evidence of their difficulty;
  • the proposed approach and alternatives;
  • access rules and the next test.

Keep the pilot to one project. Include change reporting, manager follow-up and annual declarations as one complete workflow. Leave purchasing, depreciation and automatic write-off for later. The first scope uses AI during development only.

The team expects easier reporting to keep records current and a scheduled annual check to reveal missing replies. That is the theory of change to test. Maya still needs time and authority to follow up. Better screens will have little effect if people cannot identify equipment reliably or nobody acts on reports.

Agree success before testing. For this exploratory study, at least seven of eight members should complete all three tasks correctly without help. Maya needs to find every scripted problem. Any of these results fails the test, regardless of the completion rate:

  • a change to another project’s records;
  • a handover completed without acknowledgement;
  • a declaration falsely recorded as a physical inspection.

Continue: 3 of 6 →

Output: Concept brief, alternatives, testable assumptions, baseline, target and guardrails. Next: Choose the uncertainty most likely to change the next investment and plan a test in step 3.

3. Choose the next test

Use the concept brief, comparison findings and open assumptions to choose what to learn next. Agree the question, expected result, constraints and decision rule before running the test. A draft PRD becomes useful when proposed behaviour needs more detail; an interview, sketch or technical investigation can begin without one.

Ask what evidence could change the team’s mind. Product, Design and Engineering select the greatest unresolved risk together. Use a sketch when it can answer the question; use working integration only when that is needed for credible evidence.

Record the test plan and decision criteria

The experiment owner drafts a short record from the selected question and concept brief. Product, Design and Engineering agree the plan before the test starts. Use the following suggested fields, then add findings after the test:

  1. Question and assumption: state what needs to be true and what result would challenge it. Name the user and task, or the technical or operating condition. Link the evidence that makes this question worth testing.
  2. Method and conditions: describe the task or procedure, participants or dataset, relevant access needs and comparison where needed. Identify the concept, prototype, system or draft PRD version. Record the baseline and how each measure will be collected. Link the arrangements for running and closing the test.
  3. Decision criteria and ownership: agree what would support further investment, require a change or leave the question unresolved. Set failure limits, stop conditions and a time or cost budget. Name the experiment owner, reviewer and person responsible for the next investment decision.
  4. Findings and next action: after the test, link observations to source notes or results. Record deviations from the plan, missing data and contradictory evidence. Compare findings with the agreed criteria, separate interpretation from observation, and link the decision made in step 5.

Before running the test, ask the reviewer to explain how the planned evidence could change the decision. If the method cannot distinguish the expected result from a plausible alternative explanation, revise the plan or narrow the claim.

Match the test method to the uncertainty

Choose the least costly method that can produce credible evidence for the selected question. Start with Figure 4, then use the catalogue below to check the method’s limits.

  • Is the need understood? Use interviews about recent experiences and observation of the current task. Record what people do, the difficulties they encounter and their workarounds. Stated interest alone does not show that a proposed solution helps.
  • Can people use the proposed approach? Test a sketch, clickable prototype or manually supported service on realistic tasks. Observe completion, errors, help and correction effort. Record simulated behaviour so readers can distinguish interaction findings from tested system capabilities.
  • Can the system perform within its constraints? Run a focused technical investigation or AI evaluation using representative cases, expected results and failure cases. Exercise permissions, dependencies and recovery where relevant. A successful technical test still leaves user value to investigate.
  • Does the change improve the outcome? Plan a comparison with the current workflow or another credible alternative. For a causal claim, account for task differences, learning effects and other explanations; use random allocation where appropriate and feasible. Agree the sample and analysis with someone experienced in experiment design. A small exploratory comparison can inform the next test while leaving the effect uncertain.

When one method cannot answer both a user question and a technical question, plan complementary tests and review their findings together. Record the method chosen, why it fits and what it cannot establish in the experiment record.

Reference: compare twelve experiment methods

Product School’s experimentation playbook [7] covers split tests, multivariate tests, demand probes, landing pages, usability prototypes, manual simulations, staged rollouts and adaptive personalisation. The catalogue below adds technical and operational tests, with recommended evidence limits for each.

Experiment catalogue for business and technical research
MethodQuestion and signalLimits and technical follow-up
Fake-door or smoke testQuestion and signalDoes an early-access offer attract interest? Compare eligible exposures with selections or requests to participate.

Learning example · An invitation to test asset reporting

Show eligible members a “Try reporting an asset change” link beside the current register guidance. Count how many see it and ask to join the research. When selected, explain that this is a research invitation; it does not submit an actual loss or fault report.

Limits and technical follow-upExplain availability when users select the offer. Interest does not establish sustained value, willingness to pay or build feasibility. Avoid implying that a consequential action has completed.
Landing page or message testQuestion and signalWhich value proposition attracts the intended audience? Record qualified visits, enquiries and sign-ups.

Learning example · Two messages for the same audience

Compare “Keep your assigned assets up to date” with “Report changes and complete your annual declaration”. Show the messages to comparable audiences and measure research sign-ups from eligible members and managers. Record how each audience was allocated and where it saw the message.

Limits and technical follow-upRecord the audience and acquisition channel. Recruitment bias or different traffic can explain changes; use controlled allocation when claiming one message outperforms another.
Prototype and task-based usability testQuestion and signalCan users complete the intended task? Observe comprehension, errors, completion, assistance and recovery.

Learning example · Three realistic usability tasks

In the first usability test, ask each member to:

  • hand a monitor to another member;
  • report a faulty laptop;
  • answer an annual task for an asset they cannot find.

Record whether each response is accurate and where people need help. Check keyboard access and whether Maya can follow up. Identify any actions the prototype only simulates.

Limits and technical follow-upA small qualitative study can reveal friction, but cannot estimate improvement across the user population. Note simulated behaviour and untested access needs.
Concierge testQuestion and signalDoes a service help when people deliver it openly? Observe outcomes, repeat use and the effort required to provide support.

Learning example · A manually operated reporting service

Tell participants that a coordinator will run the trial service manually. The coordinator:

  • receives reports of handovers, lost assets and faults;
  • updates a trial register with controlled access;
  • prepares the annual list of cases needing Maya’s attention.

Measure record accuracy, follow-up time and the effort needed to run the service.

Limits and technical follow-upRecord manual effort and cost. Treat this as a test of service value; separately establish whether automation can reproduce the useful result.
Wizard of Oz test
Method guidance [12]		Question and signalHow do users interact with an apparently automated interface whose responses are supplied by a person? Observe expectations and task behaviour.

Learning example · A simulated annual task queue

A researcher operates the annual task queue behind the prototype. Brief participants and explain the simulation afterwards as agreed in the research plan. Observe whether members understand their response choices. Sending reminders manually does not test whether the scheduler is reliable.

Limits and technical follow-upAgree the participant briefing and debriefing in the research plan. Keep operator responses within plausible system limits; a skilled human’s output does not validate a model or integration.
Technical spike or proof of conceptQuestion and signalCan a critical capability or integration work under specified conditions? Run an executable check and measure the relevant limits.

Learning example · A technical trial with fictional records

Import fictional asset records and check:

  • access within and across projects;
  • handovers accepted at the same time;
  • annual task creation and reminder retries;
  • behaviour around due dates.

Inspect saved records and audit history as well as the response shown on screen.

Limits and technical follow-upTest the real dependency where permitted. Record mocks, environment differences, test data, versions, failure cases and reproducible results. It does not establish demand.
Offline AI evaluationQuestion and signalCan the model or agent meet the agreed task criteria? Compare the AI with a simpler approach on cases kept separate from development and tuning.

Learning example · An offline evaluation of fault-report assistance

For an optional AI aid that sorts faults and drafts reports, use reports kept separate from development. Include unclear symptoms and descriptions containing misleading instructions. Compare its suggestions with the simple form over repeated trials. Score whether it preserves the member’s facts and whether it attempts unauthorised changes separately.

Limits and technical follow-upRecord model, prompts, data, retrieval and tool versions. Repeat variable behaviours and inspect failure cases. Offline quality does not establish adoption or production safety.
Proof-of-value pilotQuestion and signalDoes the concept improve a real workflow for a bounded group? Track task outcomes, repeat use and total service cost.

Learning example · Value testing in the pilot project

After release checks, pilot reporting in one project during an agreed declaration window. Track:

  • whether recorded holders and asset condition match the evidence;
  • follow-up on lost and faulty assets;
  • overdue replies and unresolved cases;
  • the time Maya spends managing the work.

A rehearsal with an accelerated clock cannot show how well the service works over a full year.

Limits and technical follow-upUse a credible baseline or comparator and record selection effects. Include support and correction effort; plan deeper evaluation if the pilot cannot isolate the cause of improvement.
A/B or split test
Design guidance [13]		Question and signalDoes a defined change improve a chosen outcome? Randomly allocate eligible units to control and treatment, then estimate the difference.

Learning example · A comparison across project groups

With enough eligible projects, randomly assign projects to the current reporting route or the new application. Ask an experiment specialist to agree the sample and when to stop the test. Shared assets or a manager serving both groups may affect the comparison. Measure record accuracy and follow-up as well as use of the application.

Limits and technical follow-upConfirm instrumentation, allocation unit, adequate sample and a planned stopping rule. Check guardrails and uncertainty; a small statistically detectable change may still have little practical value.
Multivariate test
Method guidance [14]		Question and signalWhich combination of factors works, and do they interact? Compare planned combinations, such as content and layout variants.

Learning example · Four layout and wording combinations

Compare two asset layouts, a list and cards, with two versions of the condition question. This gives four combinations. Collect enough observations to compare accurate completion and see whether layout changes the effect of the wording. The first study’s eight members are too few for that estimate.

Limits and technical follow-upPlan enough observations for the combinations. Use a simpler experiment when traffic is limited; changing several elements without a designed comparison obscures their effects.
Canary or beta rolloutQuestion and signalHow does an implemented change behave under limited exposure? Observe reliability, task outcomes, support demand and recovery.

Learning example · A limited release with stop conditions

Release the reviewed build to one project first. Watch for:

  • changes made without permission;
  • duplicate annual tasks or missed reminders;
  • faults left overdue;
  • failures when the background job restarts.

If writes need to stop, preserve the live register and the evidence. Monitoring a rollout does not by itself show that the application caused an improvement.

Limits and technical follow-upApply the release checks and stop criteria. Rollout monitoring alone is not a causal comparison. Keep an explicit control design when testing an improvement claim.
Adaptive personalisationQuestion and signalDoes a changing allocation policy improve outcomes across relevant users? Evaluate the policy and important segments over time.

Learning example · Adaptive reminder timing

In a later experiment, test whether changing the reminder channel or timing helps members respond. Compare it with a fixed schedule using a method suited to changing allocations. Keep contact times and opt-out rules within agreed limits, and preserve accessible routes. Members still provide their own declarations; reminder changes should not fill in answers for them.

Limits and technical follow-upUse a comparison and analysis suited to adaptive allocation, with specialist input. Set exploration limits and guardrails; automatic adaptation alone does not demonstrate benefit.

[12] explains human-controlled prototypes; [13] supports controlled-test design; [14] explains multivariate combinations. Technical spikes and AI evaluations extend the earlier feasibility guidance.

Agree how to run and close the experiment

Before testing, the experiment owner agrees these arrangements with the relevant data, security and research specialists. Resolve unclear permissions before proceeding, or choose a safer test.

  • Permitted data: identify what may be collected, entered into AI tools, stored and shared. Use synthetic or appropriately de-identified data where possible; record retention and deletion arrangements.
  • Approved tools: confirm that the tools, models and hosting are approved for the intended data and use, including how providers handle submitted information.
  • Participant information: explain the purpose, prototype limitations, AI involvement, what will be recorded and how findings will be used. Confirm consent or other applicable participation requirements and a way to withdraw or report concerns.
  • Access restrictions: define who can use the prototype, access its data or invoke connected systems. Isolate the experiment, limit permissions and agree stop conditions for unexpected effects.
  • After the experiment: name the prototype owner and expiry date. Decide how code, data and credentials will be deleted, archived or reviewed for reuse. Any promotion to production follows the applicable implementation and release checks.
Asset management journey 3 of 6 · design a test that could change the decision

Learning example · Experiment design

Check whether members can report accurately. Ask eight members to:

  • hand a monitor to another member;
  • report a faulty laptop;
  • answer an annual task for a docking station they cannot find.

Maya then reviews the reports and chooses the next action. Use fictional records and explain which actions the prototype simulates.

For every attempt, Design records:

  • whether the member completes the task accurately;
  • any mistaken confirmation that an asset is present and working;
  • help requested;
  • accessibility problems.

Rehearse comparable tasks using the spreadsheet and messages. Measure time using the interface separately from time spent on an actual inspection or repair. This small study can reveal usability problems, but it cannot estimate improvement across all users.

Test the technical questions separately. In an isolated test environment, Engineering checks:

  • imported asset identifiers and project access;
  • handovers accepted at the same time;
  • saved history of changes;
  • annual task creation and reminder dates;
  • interrupted jobs and retries.

Use a clock that the team can advance for testing. Confirm that saved responses survive a retry and each asset has one current task. Check that transfers and departing members leave outstanding work visible to Maya.

Product and Engineering estimate cost ranges for:

  • cleaning and importing the spreadsheet;
  • building and hosting the application;
  • notifications and support.

Maya confirms who can monitor the queue and arrange follow-up. Agree the research budget and stop conditions before testing. A queue with no owner, or costs above the budget, can change the investment decision.

Plan how the experiment will end. Record:

  • permitted tools and data;
  • what participants will be told;
  • access and retention arrangements;
  • the experiment owner and expiry date.

Retire test records and credentials afterwards. Advancing a test clock checks scheduling behaviour; it cannot demonstrate a year of reliable service.

Continue: 4 of 6 →

Output: Experiment record: question, method, participants or data, version, decision rule, budget and safety checks. Next: Run the agreed test in step 4; build a prototype only if the method needs one.

4. Run the test and capture findings

The experiment owner runs the agreed method and records what happened, including failed attempts and unexpected results. Preserve the plan, materials, dataset and relevant system versions so reviewers can understand the conditions. For a task-based test, observe the complete task.

When using a prototype, check it against the design system, accessibility expectations and technical constraints before involving users. Test realistic workflows across screens, roles and systems, including waiting, missing information, interruption and recovery. Include relevant experience levels and access needs. Record whose needs the sample does not cover; participant counts alone do not establish adequate evidence.

Record who owns the prototype, when it expires and what happens to it afterwards. Before reusing it in production, apply the implementation assurance checks. Include human review and correction time in the results.

Keep findings separate from proposed changes

Link observations to source notes, separate observation from interpretation and retain contradictory evidence. Record suggested changes to the concept, interaction states or draft PRD alongside the findings. Use step 5 to decide which changes the evidence supports before another test. Preserve the original decision rule; agree any revised criteria before the next test.

Generated personas, synthetic interviews and model critiques can suggest research questions. They are not observations of real users; see Nielsen Norman Group’s assessment of synthetic users [16]. Keep participant information in controlled records and link only the evidence needed for the decision.

AIHow AI can help

Generate alternatives from verified findings

After a test, use the reviewed findings to generate different responses to the same need. Keep the original observations and test criteria alongside each proposed change. Compare alternatives by the failure they address, the value assumption they test and the technical work they require.

Include a simpler or non-AI approach where useful. Engineering checks whether the new behaviour remains feasible, and Design checks the complete journey. Record candidate follow-up experiments for the decision in step 5. More generated variants are useful only when they expose a choice worth testing.

Test with the people who will use it

The Defence Product Playbook groups fast learning into four habits, which it calls TEST. The following adapts those habits to this guide’s experiment and prototype closure records:

  • Trial with real operators: test with the people who will use the product, not project team members standing in for them.
  • Expose the riskiest assumption: build only what is needed to test the assumption most likely to invalidate the proposal. Use the prototype’s recorded closure plan to retire it, retain it for research or assess it for reuse.
  • Shorten the loop: measure the time from user feedback to a changed prototype in days. If the loop is slow, fix that first.
  • Turn tests into decisions: end each test by keeping, changing or dropping the idea.
Asset management journey 4 of 6 · turn observations into a useful revision

Learning example · Findings and revisions

The first test falls short of the agreed target. Six of eight members complete all three tasks correctly without help. Two choose “all present and working” because they cannot find a clear way to report equipment that is no longer with them. Maya also cannot tell a missing item from a handover awaiting acknowledgement.

The findings show a problem with the response choices. They do not establish that members are careless or that the equipment is lost. Design gives each asset clear choices for:

  • “not with me”;
  • “faulty”;
  • “handover awaiting acknowledgement”.

Engineering checks that each answer is saved distinctly and reaches Maya’s queue.

Use the four TEST habits to guide the revision.

  • Trial with real operators: involve members and a manager;
  • Expose the riskiest assumption: include difficult cases, such as an asset the member cannot find;
  • Shorten the loop: measure the time from the finding to a revised flow;
  • Turn tests into decisions: record the decision to improve and retest before adding features.

Keep the original test materials and success criteria with the observations. AI can suggest wording based on those notes. Design checks that the revised choices make it easy to report a problem honestly.

Continue: 5 of 6 →

Output: Versioned test materials, observations, result and limitations, with proposed changes and open questions. Next: Compare evidence with the original rule in step 5 before changing the concept or running another test.

5. Decide the next investment

After each test, Product, Design and Engineering compare the findings and limitations with the agreed decision rule. Review user value, feasibility, cost, strategic fit and guardrails together. Record whether the next action is another test, a change, a pause, a stop or implementation. Agree routine follow-up experiments within the existing learning budget and delegated authority. The authorised decision owner makes any new investment commitment under local approval arrangements.

For a material investment decision, use the independent judgement check before accepting an agent-supported recommendation. A generated summary of interviews can point to a possible change, but the team still checks the original observations, considers another explanation and records what the test did not establish.

Choose one recorded outcome for the next cycle
DecisionEvidence and next move
CommitEvidence supports a defined scope, with acceptable limits and owners for unresolved questions. Agree what to build first in step 6.
Continue testingEvidence is missing or inconclusive, and does not yet justify changing the proposal. Return to step 3 with a specific question and remaining budget.
Rework: improveEvidence supports the idea, but the tested behaviour needs improvement. Confirm the change, question and decision rule in step 3 before running the revised test in step 4.
Rework: redesignThe problem remains credible but the solution is weak. Return to alternatives in step 2.
Rework: pivotThe intended user, problem or expected value changes. Return to problem framing in step 1.
DeferA temporary dependency blocks useful learning. Record its owner and a review date or reopening trigger; no implementation is authorised.
StopNo justified case remains, risk is unacceptable, or the learning budget is exhausted without support for further investment. Archive the learning and close access safely.

Check risk and budget on every loop. A harmful or prohibited experiment stops for investigation; any resumed test needs a permitted design. Neither a favourable average score nor a commitment decision waives applicable controls.

Keep investigation, implementation and release decisions distinct

Evidence for investigation, implementation and production decisions
DecisionEvidence to review
Worth investigatingA credible problem, obligation or foreseeable risk; the consequence of doing nothing; a material uncertainty; and a bounded, permitted research or experiment plan with an owner and budget.
Worth a bounded implementationEvidence supporting the chosen problem and solution under recorded conditions; feasible scope, acceptance criteria, expected value, cost and constraints; and owners for remaining uncertainties and risks.
Safe for productionEvidence from the implemented product against applicable release criteria: security, privacy, accessibility, reliability, operational readiness, monitoring and recovery, with residual risks reviewed by the authorised decision makers. Prototype results alone do not establish this.

Resolve assumptions that could invalidate the solution, or narrow the scope, before committing to implementation.

Keep reviews light and regular

Review findings when they could change the next decision. Invite other teams when the proposal affects their services or shared patterns. Two useful review formats are:

  • Focused design review: Product, Design and Engineering examine the prototype, user evidence, accessibility, design-system patterns and feasibility. Record changes and unresolved questions.
  • Cross-team review: invite people who own affected services, domain rules, shared components or controls. Ask for specific feedback on dependencies and inconsistencies. Size participation to the decision; collect input asynchronously where practical.

The decision owner records which feedback changes the proposal and why. Ask:

  1. What uncertainty did we address?
  2. What did the evidence change?
  3. What is now the highest-risk assumption?
  4. What can we now decide?

Check how the concept has changed

Before investing more, compare the proposal with the concept brief. Record changes and the evidence behind them:

  • Intent and evidence: changes to the user, problem, outcome or solution, and the findings that explain them.
  • Scope and risk: additions, removals, dependencies and changes to permissions, controls or expected value.
  • Effort and cost: updated estimates from Engineering and other relevant contributors, including ranges, assumptions and uncertainty.
  • Decision: whether the next investment remains justified, who decides and what still needs testing.

Update the brief and PRD with agreed changes. Keep earlier criteria and results so reviewers can follow the decision.

Keep human approval where the consequences exceed the organisation’s risk tolerance. Examples include material regulatory interpretation, irreversible commitments to users, security exceptions, high-impact automated actions, costly architecture decisions and deployment into sensitive domains. Widen agent autonomy only when permissions, evaluation coverage, monitoring, known failure modes and rollback make the remaining risk acceptable.

Asset management journey 5 of 6 · decide what the evidence supports

Learning example · The pilot investment decision

Improve, then test again. The team uses the remaining research budget to test the revised screens on comparable new tasks. All eight members finish correctly without help. Maya finds every scripted problem and records who will act. The same people take part again, so familiarity may explain some of the improvement.

Review the evidence from each part of Project Discovery:

  • The usability test shows members can complete the revised tasks;
  • The technical tests support project isolation, acknowledged handovers and annual tasks that survive retries;
  • The cost estimate fits the pilot budget under the recorded assumptions.

Product, Design and Engineering review these results with Maya’s capacity to follow up. A usable prototype alone cannot answer all of those questions.

Record the decision to fund the pilot. The authorised owner agrees to implement reporting and annual declarations for one project. The decision record includes:

  • the evidence and alternatives considered;
  • the agreed scope;
  • remaining questions and their owners.

This funds delivery. The release decision will need evidence from the implemented product.

How different findings would change the next move
DecisionWhat it would mean here
Continue testingWhat it would mean hereIf Maya could not attend, test manager follow-up before drawing a conclusion about the whole workflow.
ImproveWhat it would mean hereFix the unclear exception choices and repeat the relevant tasks against the original rule.
RedesignWhat it would mean hereIf a configured form or existing platform meets the full need with less cost, revisit the response rather than defending a custom app.
PivotWhat it would mean hereIf assets cannot be identified reliably, return to inventory reconciliation as the problem to investigate first.
DeferWhat it would mean hereIf identity access temporarily blocks a permitted test, name its owner and a reopening trigger.
StopWhat it would mean hereIf no acceptable access boundary or follow-up arrangement is possible, close the experiment and retain its learning.

A focused design review walks through the whole member and manager experience. A cross-team review confirms dependencies with the owners of identity, data and notifications, including who can authorise repairs. Compare the revised proposal with the brief and record what changed before committing more effort.

Continue: 6 of 6 →

Output: Dated decision, evidence links, rationale, scope changes, owners and next actions. Next: Only a delivery commitment advances to step 6; use the named return step for other outcomes.

AIHow AI can help

Ask AI to assemble the experiment findings, limitations and open questions into a draft decision brief, linked to the test records. Product, Design and Engineering check that it separates observations from interpretations; the authorised owner records the investment decision and its rationale.

6. Agree what to build first

Use the investment decision from step 5 to agree the first useful scope to build and assess. This delivery slice gives a defined user group a complete, limited capability. Product, Design and Engineering agree its boundaries together using the concept brief, experiment findings and technical and cost evidence.

  1. Define the useful outcome. Name the users, task and result this slice will support. Describe what is included and excluded, any limits on use and how the team will recognise success. Keep the scope within the conditions supported by the evidence.
  2. Make the behaviour testable. Update and version the product requirements document (PRD). Link requirements to the decision, evidence and UI or API examples. Include acceptance criteria for normal use, failure, permissions, recovery and accessibility.
  3. Resolve or assign remaining questions. Identify unknowns that could invalidate the scope or make the next work unacceptable. Return those questions to Project Discovery before dependent work proceeds. For uncertainty accepted by the decision owner, record its impact, owner, next check, budget and trigger to reconsider scope or stop.
  4. Check that implementation can begin. Use the handoff table below to compare the proposed scope with its supporting records. Ask the people taking on the work to explain the intended behaviour, evidence limits and unresolved work. Resolve conflicting requirements and missing critical inputs, then link the agreed package from the implementation tasks.

Record whether prototype code, data and credentials will be retired, retained for research or assessed for reuse, with an owner and date. Keep Product, Design and Engineering involved as implementation tests the requirements and exposes new information.

Agree how to measure the result

State how the team will judge product success after implementation, not only whether the software passes its tests. Link the plan from the PRD and include the North Star, where established, the success measure for this scope, supporting measures and guardrails. The following is a recommended handoff record:

  • Definition and scope: give each metric a name, purpose, calculation and direction of improvement. Define the people or cases counted, time window, exclusions and relevant user groups. For a rate, state both numerator and denominator; include failed or abandoned attempts where they belong.
  • Baseline and target: record the starting value, date, sample or population and source. Agree the target and review period before exposing users to the change. Keep prototype findings separate from production baselines. If a baseline is missing, record the gap, collection owner and deadline; missing data is not a zero.
  • Collection and verification: name the events, service records, research or manual checks needed, with agreed privacy and access limits. Link instrumentation work to delivery tasks. Name who checks missing events, duplicate counts and agreement between the report and source records.
  • Ownership and review: name the metric owner, collection owner, report location and review cadence. Product connects results to value, Design checks the experience and user coverage, and Engineering verifies instrumentation with data or analytics specialists where available.
  • Decision and limits: record what improvement, inconclusive evidence, a missed target or a guardrail breach will trigger. State the comparison needed to attribute improvement to the change. A rise after release alone does not establish cause; a serious breach can trigger investigation before a scheduled review.

At handoff, ask the delivery team to explain how each result will be collected and used. Resolve missing definitions, owners or critical collection work before judging the pilot or release a success. Keep open measurement questions visible with a plan to resolve them.

The measurement-plan format applies Amplitude’s metric-and-input framework [19] and draws on Microsoft’s experiment guidance [13] on hypotheses, success measures, guardrails and data quality. A measurement plan does not replace experiment design or release assurance.

Project Discovery evidence to carry into implementation
ArtefactContent to carry forwardReadiness check
Opportunity and decisionContent to carry forwardProblem, users, outcome, baseline, alternatives, selected concept and reasons; the next investment, decision owner and date.Readiness checkThe recommendation follows from the evidence, including conflicting findings and rejected options.
PRD and experienceContent to carry forwardBounded scope, exclusions, stories, acceptance criteria, quality targets and UI artefacts or representative API interactions.Readiness checkThe intended behaviour is testable, including failure, permission, recovery and accessibility cases.
Validation evidenceContent to carry forwardAssumptions, test criteria, method, participants or datasets, versions, results, limitations and evidence links.Readiness checkSupported, unsupported and inconclusive claims are distinct; tests cover the highest-risk business and technical assumptions.
Technical findingsContent to carry forwardSystem and data-flow context, approach options, spike results, dependency confirmations, initial architecture decisions and build/run cost ranges.Readiness checkEngineering can explain why the bounded scope appears feasible and which conditions limit that conclusion.
Remaining uncertaintyContent to carry forwardRisk or unknown, potential impact, owner, next check, time or cost bound, and trigger to reconsider scope or stop.Readiness checkBlocking unknowns return to Project Discovery. Any accepted uncertainty has an explicit resolution and escalation route.
Delivery and measurementContent to carry forwardThe first useful slice and product measurement plan: North Star where established, scoped success measures, definitions, baselines, targets, guardrails, collection tasks, owners and review decisions.Readiness checkThe delivery team can explain how success will be measured after use, plan instrumentation and data checks, and identify when findings should reopen Project Discovery.

For AI-assisted findings that affect a decision, retain the checked source extract, model or tool version, instructions and reviewer. Link the finding to the decision and restrict access as needed. Label generated scenarios and discarded interpretations so delivery can distinguish them from user evidence.

Asset management journey 6 of 6 · agree a complete first delivery slice

Learning example · The first delivery scope

Describe the complete first release. For one project:

  • Maya checks the opening spreadsheet against the evidence and assigns assets;
  • Members record acknowledged handovers and report loss or faults;
  • A yearly schedule opens declaration tasks and sends agreed reminders;
  • Maya sees overdue replies and reports that need follow-up.
Carry meaningful requirements and checks into delivery
RequirementHow the team will check it
Keep access within the project and roleHow the team will check itTry both allowed and denied actions as a member and as a manager. Confirm that a denied request leaves records unchanged and reveals no unrelated project data.
Change the holder after acknowledgementHow the team will check itAlex starts the monitor handover and Priya acknowledges it. Repeat the acceptance and try a conflicting one. The asset still has one current holder, with an accurate history.
Preserve annual tasks and responses on retryHow the team will check itSave a declaration reporting a faulty asset. Interrupt the yearly job, then run it again. Confirm there is still one current task and the saved response remains visible.
Keep lost and faulty reports actionableHow the team will check itCheck that the report stays linked to the asset and appears in Maya’s queue. It needs an owner and a visible follow-up status. Reporting a loss or fault leaves removal and repair as separate actions.
Record declarations honestlyHow the team will check itKeep each response distinct:
  • not with me;
  • faulty;
  • lost;
  • handover awaiting acknowledgement.
Keep missing replies overdue. Record physical inspections separately from member declarations.

Carry the evidence into delivery. Keep these records linked:

  • reviewed requirements and exception screens;
  • research and usability test results;
  • technical findings and cost assumptions.

Engineering owns the remaining production checks for identity, imports and recovery. Maya confirms the annual schedule and follow-up owner. Resolve unclear starting assignments before issuing member tasks.

Plan how to measure the pilot. Product proposes measuring the share of assets whose holder and condition agree with the evidence and whose reported problems have a recorded resolution. Use the annual check’s asset roster as the denominator. Show these separately:

  • handovers still awaiting acknowledgement;
  • lost or faulty items awaiting action;
  • overdue replies.

A higher submission count should not hide a less accurate register.

Measure the current workflow before setting pilot targets. Record:

  • outdated assignments;
  • Maya’s time spent chasing replies;
  • time from a fault report to follow-up.

Agree numerical targets and a review period before the pilot goes live; the brief provides neither. Engineering plans data collection and checks for duplicate or missing events. Product owns the report, Design checks whose experience it covers, and Maya follows up the queue. Observe an actual annual cycle before claiming a yearly benefit.

Continue with planning and delivery →

For products using agents at runtime, include the tested limits on actions, approval points, failure and recovery cases, and evaluation results. Link each to intended behaviour and acceptance criteria.

The table above is Project Discovery’s detailed handoff checklist. Use the overview’s handoff agreement to understand the lifecycle connection, then apply the implementation readiness checks to the scope being changed. Link the same records across these checks instead of creating separate copies. Implementation develops the technical design, tasks, verification and release evidence.

If implementation uncovers a bounded defect, correct it in that loop. If evidence challenges the user, problem, value or intended behaviour, return to the appropriate Project Discovery step and record the change. Use the overview’s feedback signals and decisions to diagnose unclear outcomes and coordinate the response. Feedback does not automatically authorise model retraining or wider permissions.

Output: Versioned evidence-backed PRD, linked evidence and a product measurement plan, with owners for remaining questions. Next: Confirm implementation can collect the agreed measures; release requires evidence from the implemented product.

Optional deep dives

Use these references when a learning question needs more detail. Return to the relevant step with the findings; these references do not add mandatory stages.

Reference: test technical assumptions as concepts emerge

Test feasibility alongside user value

Use SVPG’s feasibility risk [3] to ask whether the available people, time and technology can deliver a candidate solution. Engineering leads the investigation with Product, Design and the affected service owners. Use this checklist as candidate concepts emerge and revisit it when scope or conditions change.
