Technical assumptions to resolve before a bounded commitment
AssumptionCheck and retained evidence
The critical path can workCheck and retained evidenceCompare reuse, purchase and build options. Exercise the uncertain interface or capability; retain executable results, versions, dependency owners and untested conditions.

Learning example · A complete task across three solutions

Compare the same complete task in:

  • a managed form;
  • a configured asset platform;
  • a custom application.

Follow an imported assignment through a member’s report to Maya’s follow-up. Separately check the background job that opens annual declarations.

Data and actions are permittedCheck and retained evidenceTest identity, data access and action boundaries with representative permitted and denied cases. Record missing access and decisions needed from accountable owners.

Learning example · Project access after changes

Use fictional members and managers in two projects to check:

  • access to their own project’s records;
  • denied access to another project’s records;
  • access after an asset changes holder;
  • access after a member leaves.

Keep the allowed and denied results with the audit history. Exclude unrelated member details.

The service can meet operating limitsCheck and retained evidenceMeasure relevant latency, volume, failure and recovery behaviour. State test conditions, quality targets and differences from the intended environment.

Learning example · Annual scheduling and retry checks

Use a controlled clock and simulate job interruptions and notification failures. Check that:

  • each annual run keeps the same identity on retry;
  • each asset has one current task and saved responses survive retries;
  • due dates work as intended;
  • a transfer during the annual check reaches the correct person.

Record software versions and test load, and explain how the environment differs from production.

Delivery and operation are affordableCheck and retained evidenceEstimate build, integration, migration, support and exit costs as ranges. Confirm skills, capacity and external lead times; record assumptions and sensitivity.

Learning example · Pilot cost ranges

Estimate a range for each cost:

  • cleaning and importing spreadsheet data;
  • configuring an existing platform or building the application;
  • connecting identity and notification services;
  • hosting and supporting the service;
  • following up reports.

Check whether a higher migration estimate would put the pilot over its agreed budget.

AI adds useful capability, where proposedCheck and retained evidenceCompare the AI with a simpler approach on representative cases kept separate from development and tuning. Retain model, prompt and data versions, failure cases, human correction effort and cost per successful task.

Learning example · AI drafting compared with a simple form

The core application records the holder and condition in structured fields. Compare any optional AI drafting aid with that form. Check:

  • urgent faults it misses;
  • facts it invents or changes;
  • the corrections members need to make;
  • the cost of each useful report after review.

If an important technical question remains open, run a short investigation, often called a spike. Agree its question, owner, test environment, success criteria and budget. Report what ran, what failed and what remains unknown. A simulated integration tests the interaction; test the real dependency separately and carry findings into the technical requirements document (TRD).

Reference: use the Double Diamond to widen and narrow choices
Reference: Project Discovery frameworks

Choose a framework for the question

A framework organises Project Discovery work; a method gathers evidence about a particular question. Use the six steps above as the shared process, and choose frameworks within them. Product School’s Project Discovery guide [6] introduces six useful approaches: dual-track discovery and delivery, Jobs To Be Done, Double Diamond, Design Sprint, Lean Startup and Opportunity Solution Trees.

The table shows where each approach helps and the working artefact to retain. Use the originating sources for each framework; the JTBD row also links the Christensen Institute’s account [18]. Investigate feasibility and review the evidence whichever framework you use.

Project Discovery frameworks and how to apply them
FrameworkUse and working artefactTechnical investigation connection
Continuous discovery and delivery
SVPG [10]		Use and working artefactUse when learning continues alongside implementation. The same Product, Design and Engineering contributors investigate upcoming options while delivery develops bounded, supported scope. Keep a shared learning backlog and decision record. Cagan’s article now favours continuous discovery and delivery over its older “Dual-track Agile” label, to emphasise principles rather than process.

Learning example · Research alongside delivery

While Engineering builds the pilot project, Product and Design investigate:

  • how shared equipment is recorded;
  • what happens when members leave;
  • whether Maya can keep up with follow-up.

Add import and scheduling findings to the same research backlog. Record decisions about material changes to scope.

Technical investigation connectionRoute integration, operating-cost and quality findings back into Project Discovery. Keep collaboration active through handover; separate workstreams do not require separate teams.
Jobs To Be Done
Christensen Institute [18]		Use and working artefactUse when the underlying need is unclear. Investigate the circumstances, the progress users seek, its functional, social and emotional dimensions, and why current alternatives fall short. Retain an evidence-linked job statement.

Learning example · The job behind an asset report

Ask a member about a recent handover and Maya about chasing annual replies. A possible job statement is: “When an asset changes hands or develops a fault, I need to record the change and know who will follow up.” Ask how much effort reporting takes, how confident people feel and whether fear of blame affects reports of loss.

Technical investigation connectionExplore constraints in the user’s actual setting, including access, devices, connectivity and workarounds. Keep the desired outcome independent of a preferred technology.
Double Diamond
Design Council [2]		Use and working artefactUse when the team is converging too early. Discover and Define expand and narrow the problem; Develop and Deliver explore and test responses. Retain problem and concept alternatives with reasons for narrowing them.

Learning example · Double Diamond for asset reporting

Apply the Double Diamond to the reporting problem:

  • Discover how members use spreadsheets, messages and physical checks;
  • Define the difficulty those observations support;
  • Develop alternatives using a form, an existing platform or an application;
  • Test a small version of the most promising approach.

Revisit the problem if assets cannot be identified reliably or nobody has capacity to follow up.

Technical investigation connectionExplore reuse, process changes and different technical approaches before commitment. See the Double Diamond explanation.
Design Sprint
GV [11]		Use and working artefactUse for a focused question with available participants and decision makers. The five-day format maps the challenge, sketches options, chooses a direction, prototypes and tests it. Retain the storyboard, prototype and observations.

Learning example · A five-day reporting sprint

Use the five-day sprint to focus on the member and manager experience:

  • Monday: map the current journey;
  • Tuesday: sketch possible solutions;
  • Wednesday: choose a storyboard;
  • Thursday: build the prototype;
  • Friday: test it with users.

Investigate the annual background job separately; the prototype screens simulate its behaviour.

Technical investigation connectionInvolve Engineering in choosing the testable slice. Run a separate spike for simulated integrations; the sprint’s prototype findings do not settle implementation feasibility.
Lean Startup
Build–Measure–Learn [9]		Use and working artefactUse repeated learning cycles when the value proposition or operating model is uncertain. Choose an assumption, build the smallest credible test, measure the result and decide whether to persevere or change direction. Retain the hypothesis, measures and decision.

Learning example · A small build–measure–learn cycle

Build the smallest flow that lets members report changes and answer an annual task. Check whether members can report accurately and Maya can find their reports. Revise the flow after the first test, then test again. Collect separate evidence for the service’s annual benefit and readiness for live use.

Technical investigation connectionInclude build, run and support cost in the learning. A minimum viable product (MVP) used by real users still needs the controls appropriate to its data, actions and exposure.
Opportunity Solution Tree
Teresa Torres [8]		Use and working artefactUse to connect a desired outcome to researched user opportunities, alternative solutions and assumption tests. Retain the tree and links to evidence; compare several responses to the selected opportunity.

Learning example · An opportunity tree for accurate records

Start with the outcome of a current, reliable register. Investigate three opportunities:

  • handovers that never reach the register;
  • fault reports left in messages;
  • annual checks that depend on Maya starting them manually.

Compare the form, platform and application options. Link each option to the interview, usability test or technical check that tests its key assumption.

Technical investigation connectionAttach feasibility assumptions and spike results to solution branches. Keep user opportunities distinct from implementation tasks or a list of requested features.

Combine only the practices the decision needs

For a complex question, interviews can clarify the task, an opportunity tree can organise alternative responses, and a focused sprint can test an interaction. Use Build–Measure–Learn to repeat the experiments and continuous discovery to keep learning connected to delivery. Record the question, evidence and next decision rather than treating framework completion as progress.

When agents use the product: test their journey

Test the experience when an agent acts for a user

When the product will be operated by AI agents, test that interaction during Project Discovery. Sumit Sheth calls this agentic user experience (AUX): designing how agents use a product alongside its human experience. Exposing an API alone does not establish a useful journey.

The following are suggested Project Discovery checks for such products. For software that only uses AI during development, continue with the usual user and service journeys.

Suggested checks for a journey carried out by an agent
Part of the journeyWhat to test
Intent and contextCan the agent identify the intended task, obtain permitted context and ask for missing information without inventing it?

Learning example · Missing details in a fault report

A member tells the optional assistant, “My assigned monitor is faulty.” The assistant needs the asset ID and observed symptoms before drafting the report. It asks for missing details and keeps any diagnosis or inspection claim out of the report unless supported.

Permission and controlCan the user see the proposed action, set its scope, give any required approval and stop further work?

Learning example · Member confirmation before submission

Show the draft fault report to the member and ask whether to submit it. If the member declines, save no report. Keep actions on other people’s assets and repair purchases outside the assistant’s agreed permissions.

Action and resultCan the agent choose the appropriate operation and distinguish a completed task from a request that was merely accepted?

Learning example · Report status and repair status

Check that the assistant distinguishes these recorded states:

  • a draft awaiting confirmation;
  • a submitted fault report;
  • follow-up assigned to Maya;
  • a completed repair.

A submission confirmation does not mean the repair is complete.

Failure and recoveryWhat happens after a timeout, partial completion, ambiguous instruction or denied access? Check that a retry does not duplicate a consequential action.

Learning example · Recovery after a submission timeout

After a timeout, look up the report using its request ID before retrying. Check for:

  • a duplicate fault report;
  • a change to the wrong asset;
  • an asset transferred to another member;
  • access revoked while the task was running.
Explanation and handbackCan the user inspect what changed, correct the result, recover where possible and take over with enough context?

Learning example · Member correction and manager takeover

Let the member read and correct the report. If Maya takes over, give her the original description, current status and history. Preserve a reported problem until someone resolves it; never silently change it to “present and working”.

Learning example · An optional fault-report assistant

For a later, optional reporting assistant, test whether it can draft a fault report and submit it after the member confirms. Include:

  • a missing asset ID;
  • unclear symptoms;
  • a member declining submission;
  • an asset transferred to another member;
  • a timeout after the report is accepted.

Check that it asks for missing information and looks up the saved report before retrying. Inspect both the report and Maya’s queue. Record invented details, duplicate reports and the effort needed to take over. This feature remains outside the reviewed PRD. It cannot confirm a physical inspection or submit an annual declaration without the member’s knowledge.

Record the model, tool interface, permissions and test conditions with the prototype version. Repeat variable behaviours and inspect the resulting system state. Use the AI evaluation guidance to plan deeper checks during implementation.

Inspiration: [5] on AUX.

Advanced: link intent, decisions and requirements

Product intent explains why a product exists, what it should do and which limits apply. Keep the evidence, requirements, designs, decisions and open questions linked. Review contradictions before using these records as context for an agent.

Link the intended outcomes to product behaviour and the architecture that supports it. Show how policy and evaluation apply across those links:

  • a product behaviour exists because it supports a user and business outcome;
  • an architecture choice exists because it enables required behaviour under known constraints;
  • a policy control exists because it addresses a defined risk; and
  • an evaluation shows whether the intended behaviour and constraints are met.

Keep product intent versioned, owned, accessible and auditable. Where practical, make the most valuable parts machine-readable: API descriptions, schemas, policy rules, acceptance tests and evaluation datasets can be checked automatically, not only read.

Learning example · Links from requirements to tests

An accurate register depends on two requirements: visible member updates and reliable annual declarations. The design gives each asset one current task in each annual check. The retry test checks whether a saved declaration survives another run. The access test checks whether a member can change only the records they are permitted to use.

Link the requirements and design to the reviewed data structures and executable tests. When a handover rule changes, review:

  • the affected screens;
  • handling during an annual check;
  • the related acceptance tests.

Update the information supplied to agents after those records agree.

Record feedback and decisions between meetings

Attach feedback to a specific version of the brief, prototype or PRD. State the question, response deadline and decision owner. Keep one linked decision record with the date, options considered, evidence, rationale, actions and superseded decisions.

Link relevant comments and discussion notes from that record. Check AI-generated summaries against the original notes before relying on them, and confirm material decisions with their owners. Use recordings only where permitted, with agreed access and retention.

Learning example · A decision about a departing member

Maya asks what happens if a member leaves during the annual check. Attach her comment to PRD v0.3 and name the decision owner and response deadline. Record whether the outstanding task returns to Maya, explain the reason and update the affected tests. AI can summarise the discussion; Product checks the original comment and confirms the decision before publishing the revised PRD. Keep the earlier rule in the history and limit access to member details.

A useful specification makes assumptions, constraints, permissions, non-functional requirements, edge cases and exclusions explicit. Increase precision as uncertainty falls, and revise intent when evidence changes. Read about spec-driven development. GitHub Spec Kit’s methodology [4] advocates versioned specifications, linked technical plans and feedback from implementation; treat this as a proposed method and verify generated code against the requirements.

Advanced: connect measures to value

Draw on several kinds of evidence

  • User evidence: interviews, usability studies, support cases and co-creation sessions.
  • Behavioural evidence: product analytics, controlled experiments, workflow completion and adoption.
  • Operational evidence: telemetry, reliability, latency, incidents, model traces and recovery.
  • Evaluation evidence: offline datasets, automated tests, agent evaluations, policy checks and calibrated model-based judges.
  • Cost evidence: experiment cost, delivery effort, inference cost and the human attention consumed.

Use AI summaries to find themes worth checking against the original feedback. A summary does not establish cause, and an evaluation score covers only the cases and criteria used. Read how to evaluate AI behaviour and check model-based judgements.

Link each result to its research notes, dataset or test run. Keep participant information in the appropriate controlled location and summarise only what the decision needs. When evidence conflicts, record the conflict rather than averaging it into a reassuring conclusion.

Product, Design and Engineering should review feedback from use together. If evidence challenges the user need or intended behaviour, reopen Project Discovery; if it reveals a bounded implementation defect, route it to delivery. Change the product intent through a recorded decision; feedback does not automatically authorise model retraining or broader agent permissions.

Connect the measures chosen in Frame

Features shipped, prototypes generated, prompts submitted and lines of AI-generated code measure activity. They do not show user impact or business value. Define measures at each of these layers:

Suggested measurement layers; set local measures and thresholds before testing
LayerWhat it answers
User outcomeDid the user achieve the outcome that makes the product worthwhile?

Learning example · Successful reporting and follow-up

Can members accurately report who holds an asset and whether it works? Can Maya find the report and resolve the issue without information getting lost between channels?

Business outcomeDid the product create the intended value for the organisation?

Learning example · Value to the organisation

Investigate whether the application helps achieve:

  • a more accurate register;
  • earlier inspection or repair follow-up;
  • less time spent chasing annual replies.

Collect evidence before claiming that it reduces asset loss or saves money.

Product behaviourDid users adopt the behaviour that should drive the outcome?

Learning example · Reporting behaviours to track

Track the work across both the application and previous reporting channels:

  • acknowledged handovers;
  • reports of lost or faulty assets;
  • annual responses;
  • Maya’s follow-up actions.
Leading indicatorsAre early signals moving in the expected direction?

Learning example · Early signals of improvement

Track these early signals:

  • time between an asset change and its report;
  • reminders successfully delivered;
  • annual tasks completed.

Check whether they are associated with more accurate holder and condition records. An increase alone does not establish value.

Learning speed and costHow quickly and affordably did a hypothesis become credible evidence and a decision?

Learning example · Time and cost of reaching a decision

Follow the reporting question through both usability tests to the pilot decision. Record:

  • total elapsed time;
  • time contributed by members, Maya and the research team;
  • prototype, engineering and review costs.
GuardrailsDid quality, safety, reliability, cost, privacy and fairness stay within tolerance?

Learning example · Failures reported separately

Report important failures separately:

  • changes to another project’s records;
  • a declaration incorrectly labelled as a physical inspection;
  • missed annual checks or duplicate tasks;
  • faults left without follow-up;
  • accessibility problems;
  • costs above the agreed limit.

Choose a value measure to steer by

Use this adaptation of the Defence Product Playbook’s four-rung ladder to connect resources and early signals to value and longer-term outcomes. Here, “input” means resources invested; the playbook uses it for logins, uptime and shipped features. See the source-adaptation note.

The metric ladder, adapted from the Defence Product Playbook
RungWhat it shows
1. Input measureResources invested, such as team effort, funding or compute

Learning example · Resources used by the pilot

Record the resources used for the reporting and annual-check pilot:

  • delivery and research time;
  • spreadsheet cleanup effort;
  • test notifications and hosting costs.
2. Leading indicatorAn early behaviour change that supports part of the theory of change

Learning example · Behaviour linked to accurate records

Check whether more members acknowledge handovers and submit accurate declarations on time. Then check whether those actions lead to current records and completed follow-up.

3. Value measureThe intended outcome of solving the problem; the measure the team steers by

Learning example · A measure of reliable asset records

Measure the share of assets in scope whose holder and condition have been checked against evidence and whose reported problems have a recorded resolution. Report completion, overdue work and effort alongside that measure.

4. Outcome measureThe effect the organisation ultimately seeks; often slower to change than measures used to guide weekly work

Learning example · Equipment availability and wider outcomes

Check whether the team can account for project equipment and use it when needed. Include the time taken to arrange inspections and repairs. Establish that connection before crediting the application with reducing loss or disruption.

Higher rungs aim to measure effects closer to the intended value, but confidence still depends on evidence quality and the causal link between measures. The playbook recommends one value measure per problem that can move at least twice a year. This describes how often meaningful change can be observed. Explain how improving the measure contributes to the outcome above it, and test that relationship. Choose a review cadence suited to the product and decision, and carry it into the measurement plan.

Uptime is an operational reliability measure. Depending on the product, it may be a guardrail, a service outcome or a direct contributor to mission value. Usage can be a leading indicator when evidence links it to the intended outcome. Neither is naturally a resource input, and neither alone demonstrates that the problem is being solved.

Ask whether the measure could improve while the intended outcome stays unchanged. Check the link between them. Keep useful operational measures and, unlike the playbook, consider self-reported outcomes such as satisfaction, effort and trust. Compare these with observed behaviour and service data, noting sampling and response biases. Check that measures are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound (SMART).

The playbook’s value-cost ratio measures outcome delivered per annual cost and tracks change year on year. State the outcome units, costs included and measurement period. Compare ratios only when those units and cost boundaries are comparable, or a justified common valuation makes comparison possible. Financial return on investment (ROI) also needs justified monetary benefits and costs.

When measured value plateaus, investigate whether the product is sustaining an essential outcome or meeting an obligation before shifting investment. Maintenance may preserve mission value, supportability and risk controls even when the headline measure no longer rises.

Learning example · SMART targets and service efficiency

Use SMART to make the pilot target clear:

  • Specific: name the project and reporting window;
  • Measurable: compare results against the versioned asset roster;
  • Achievable: account for Maya’s capacity to follow up;
  • Relevant: measure accurate holder and condition records;
  • Time-bound: agree due dates and a review date.

Collect a baseline before setting numerical improvement targets. More completed declarations are not a success if they hide lost or faulty assets.

For a later fictional cost comparison, use the same scope and cost boundaries:

  • 80 reconciled records per month at S$400 total service cost gives 0.20 records per dollar;
  • 100 records at S$450 gives about 0.222 records per dollar;
  • That is about an 11% improvement in records per dollar.

This measures service efficiency, not financial return on investment. If all records are already reconciled, keep essential reporting and audit functions working before moving investment elsewhere.

Measures worth considering include:

  • Time to validated learning: elapsed time from an explicit hypothesis to credible evidence and a decision.

    Learning example · Time to a reviewed learning decision

    Measure the time from asking whether members can declare accurately to the reviewed decision after the second usability test.

  • Cost per experiment: the cost of producing credible learning, including compute and human review.

    Learning example · The full cost of two test cycles

    Include the full cost of both test cycles:

    • participation by members and Maya;
    • research and prototype work;
    • technical investigations and computing;
    • review and corrections.
  • Human attention ratio: the share of team time spent on users, strategy, judgement, difficult exceptions and learning, rather than producing documents and coordinating.

    Learning example · Time spent learning and coordinating

    Use the same total team time when comparing effort spent learning with effort spent documenting and coordinating. Count observation and decisions based on evidence consistently, so the comparison is meaningful.

  • Product guardrails: task success, correction and escalation rates, model errors, latency, reliability, cost, privacy and safety incidents, fairness where material, and user trust.

    Learning example · Product limits alongside outcomes

    Monitor these limits alongside the outcome measures:

    • unauthorised changes;
    • missed or duplicate annual tasks;
    • unresolved faults or false inspection records;
    • slow responses and excessive costs;
    • loss of user trust.

    Investigate serious individual failures even when the averages improve.

Measurement source: Defence Product Playbook [1], “Define the problem, measure the value”.
